desc:
nums is a permutation of the integers 1..n (each appears exactly once) and k is one of those values. Count the non-empty subarrays whose median equals k.

The median of a list is the middle element after sorting it. For an even-length list, take the left of the two middle elements. For example the median of [2, 3, 1, 4] is 2 and the median of [5, 2, 3] is 3.

nums = [3, 2, 1, 4, 5], k = 4
subarrays: [4], [4, 5], [1, 4, 5]
result = 3
hints: Any qualifying subarray must contain the position of k. Compare every other element only with k: greater, or smaller.

Give each element a score: +1 if greater than k, -1 if smaller, 0 for k itself. A subarray containing k has median k when the total score is 0 (odd length) or 1 (even length, since the left middle must be k).

Split at the position of k. Count, with a hash map, how many ways the left part (ending just before k, possibly empty) can have each score, then for every right part (starting at k, extending right) add the number of left parts that bring the total to 0 or 1.
editorial: Because all values are distinct, 'median is k' depends only on how many elements are greater and how many are smaller than k. If a subarray contains k, let g and s be the counts of greater and smaller elements. The sorted order puts k at index s, and the (left) median is at index (len - 1) / 2 with len = g + s + 1. This equals s exactly when g - s is 0 or 1.

Walk left from the position of k, accumulating the balance (+1 for greater, -1 for smaller) and count how many left extensions give each balance (the empty extension has balance 0). Then walk right from k, again accumulating the balance, and for each right extension (including the one that stops at k) add left[-b] + left[1 - b]. The total is O(n) time and O(n) space; a brute force over all subarrays with sorting would take O(n3 log n).
